title: Observability
description: Seeing across services: tracing, OpenTelemetry, SLOs, alerting and incident response.
resumo: Traces follow one request across services; propagate `traceparent` with the auto-configured clients.
OpenTelemetry: instrument once, send to a Collector, choose backends freely — agent or Micrometer bridge, not both.
SLI = what you measure, SLO = internal target, SLA = contract; the error budget decides speed vs stability. Never a 100% SLO.
Alert on user-facing symptoms with a runbook; require minimum traffic so low volume does not page.
Incidents: mitigate first (rollback), investigate after; blameless postmortems.

subsections.subtitle: Distributed Tracing
subsections.description: Following one request through many services.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** checkout takes 900 ms and touches five services. Logs from each service tell you nothing about where the time went.

**Concept:** a trace represents one complete request; each operation in it (an HTTP call, a SQL query, a message) is a span with a start, a duration and attributes. The context travels between services in headers (`traceparent`, the W3C standard), and tools such as Jaeger, Tempo or Zipkin assemble the span tree — showing that 700 of the 900 ms were spent in the shipping service.

**How it works:** use sampling to control cost: keeping every trace of a busy system is expensive, and a sample is usually enough to find bottlenecks.
examples.code:
GET /checkout  ─────────────────────────────── 900ms
  ├─ api-orders: SELECT cart ───────── 40ms
  ├─ api-shipping: GET /shipping/01001000 ──── 700ms   <- bottleneck
  └─ api-payments: POST /charges ────── 120ms

traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01
examples.interview_question: How does tracing help find bottlenecks between services?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Calling another service with a client that does not propagate the context. The trace breaks in two, and the slow call shows up as an unrelated trace. Use the instrumented client beans (`RestClient.Builder`, `WebClient.Builder`) that Spring Boot configures, instead of creating clients by hand.

subsections.subtitle: OpenTelemetry
subsections.description: One open standard for logs, metrics and traces.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** each observability vendor has its own SDK; switching vendors means changing code in every service.

**Concept:** OpenTelemetry defines APIs, SDKs and a protocol (OTLP) for the three signals, independent of any vendor. The application is instrumented once and sends data to an OpenTelemetry Collector, which routes it to Prometheus, Jaeger, Datadog or any other backend — changing tools needs no code changes. The Java agent instruments HTTP, JDBC and Kafka automatically; in Spring Boot, Micrometer Tracing with the OTel bridge plays the same role.

**How it works:** the Collector can also filter, sample and enrich data before it reaches the (paid) backend.
examples.code:
# Java agent: automatic instrumentation, no code changes
java -javaagent:opentelemetry-javaagent.jar \
     -Dotel.service.name=api-orders \
     -Dotel.exporter.otlp.endpoint=http://otel-collector:4317 \
     -jar app.jar
examples.interview_question: Why adopt OpenTelemetry instead of a vendor SDK?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Running the Java agent and Micrometer Tracing's OTel bridge at the same time. Both instrument the same calls, producing duplicate spans and conflicting context. Choose one approach per service.
examples.code:
# WRONG: agent + micrometer-tracing-bridge-otel in the same app
java -javaagent:opentelemetry-javaagent.jar -jar app.jar   # app also depends on the bridge

# RIGHT: either the agent, or Micrometer Tracing — not both

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** is 99.5% availability good? Without an agreed target, every incident starts an argument about whether it matters.

**Concept:** an SLI is the measured indicator (for example, the share of requests that succeed in under 300 ms). An SLO is the internal target for it (99.9% over 30 days). An SLA is the contractual commitment to customers, with penalties — usually looser than the SLO. The error budget is how much you may fail (0.1% ≈ 43 minutes a month): with budget left, the team speeds up releases; when it is spent, it prioritizes stability.

**How it works:** compute long windows with Prometheus recording rules rather than querying 30 days of raw data each time.
examples.code:
SLI:  requests with status < 500 and latency < 300 ms / all requests
SLO:  99.9% over a rolling 30-day window
Error budget: 0.1% of 30 days ≈ 43 min of unavailability

# PromQL: no 5xx AND under 300 ms over 30 days
# (requires the 300 ms bucket: management.metrics.distribution.slo.http.server.requests=300ms)
sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_bucket{le="0.3", status!~"5.."}[30d]))
  / sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count[30d]))
examples.interview_question: What is the difference between an SLI, an SLO and an SLA?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: An SLO of 100%. It leaves no error budget, so every deploy is a risk to the target, releases slow down, and real systems never meet it anyway. Pick the reliability users actually need.
examples.code:
WRONG: SLO 100% -> zero budget -> every change is "too risky"

RIGHT: 99.9% for checkout, 99% for the recommendations panel —
       each SLO matched to what users notice

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** the on-call phone rings fifty times a night for "CPU above 80%", so the one alert that matters is ignored.

**Concept:** alert on symptoms that affect users — error rate, latency, fast error-budget burn — rather than on every possible cause (CPU at 80%). Every alert must be actionable and have a runbook saying what to do. Use windows and thresholds that ignore spikes of a few seconds, and review alerts that fire without needing action: ignored alerts hide the important ones.

**How it works:** `for:` makes the condition hold for a while before firing; `severity` decides whether it pages someone or just opens a ticket.
examples.code:
# Prometheus: error rate above 2% for 5 minutes
groups:
  - name: api-orders
    rules:
      - alert: HighErrorRate
        expr: |
          sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{status=~"5.."}[5m]))
            / sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count[5m])) > 0.02
        for: 5m
        labels: { severity: page }
        annotations:
          runbook: https://wiki.shop/runbooks/api-orders-errors
examples.interview_question: How do you avoid alert fatigue?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: An error-rate alert with no minimum traffic. At 3 a.m., one failed request out of two is a 50% error rate, and someone is woken up for nothing. Require a minimum request rate in the expression.
examples.code:
# WRONG: 1 error out of 2 requests = 50% -> page
sum(rate(...{status=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(...[5m])) > 0.02

# RIGHT: only alert when there is real traffic
(sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{status=~"5.."}[5m]))
   / sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count[5m])) > 0.02)
and sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count[5m])) > 1

subsections.subtitle: Dashboards and Incident Investigation
subsections.description: From the alert to the root cause.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** an alert fires, and the team jumps between dashboards and log searches without a plan while users wait.

**Concept:** start with the service dashboard (the golden signals) and correlate with events: was there a deploy, a traffic spike, a configuration change? Use metrics to narrow down when and where, traces to find the slow span, and the logs for that traceId for the detail. Mitigate first (roll back, scale), investigate afterwards, and write a blameless postmortem with actions to prevent a repeat.

**How it works:** mark deploys on the dashboards: most incidents start right after a change.
examples.code:
1. Alert: checkout p99 > 2s
2. Dashboard: started at 14:05, together with the v1.4.0 deploy
3. Traces: the "SELECT orders" span went from 20ms to 1.5s
4. Logs for that traceId: a new query without an index on orders.status
5. Mitigation: roll back to v1.3.9
6. Fix: add the index + a performance test in CI
7. Blameless postmortem with actions and owners
examples.interview_question: How do you investigate a latency increase in production?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Debugging the root cause while users are still affected. The fix might take hours; a rollback takes minutes. Stop the damage first, then investigate with the evidence you kept.
examples.code:
WRONG: 40 minutes reading code to understand the bug, errors still at 30%

RIGHT: 14:07 roll back -> 14:09 errors back to normal
       -> investigate with the traces and logs from 14:05-14:07
